title: 1 Rook VS 2 Pawns
summary: Delay the king approach so that the enemy pawn vacates a mating line at exactly the right moment.

nodes.question: Why wait with Ke7 before approaching the black king?
nodes.explanation: White can attack the exposed king instead of trying to stop both connected passers directly. The timing of their advance changes whether the rook can deliver mate.

nodes.question: Does promotion save Black?
nodes.explanation: The d-pawn has fallen, leaving a pawn on e2. Its promotion opens the second rank for a winning rook transfer; after queen promotion, Black can interpose once before actual mate.

branches.title: Wait, blockade, then use promotion to deliver mate
commentary: Begin from the full five-piece saved diagram. White must combine defense against promotion with threats against Kh7.
Ke7 delays Kf7 by one move. White lets the pawns advance before setting up the mating net.
d3 advances the rear pawn and keeps e3 protected. This is the source’s selected pawn reply.
Kf7 now restricts the black king, controlling g8, g7 and g6.
d2 brings the pawn to the seventh rank, where a rook blockade becomes urgent.
Rd6 stops the d-pawn from behind while preparing to capture it if the e-pawn advances.
e2 threatens promotion but releases the protection of d2. It also places the pawn on the rook’s eventual second-rank route.
Rxd2 removes the d-pawn. White threatens to collect e2 if Black spends a tempo moving the king.
e1=Q promotes, vacating e2 and opening the entire second rank. Black gets a queen but loses the ability to block that route.
Rh2+ uses the newly cleared rank. Kf7 covers g6, g7 and g8, but this is not yet mate: the new queen can interpose on h4.
Qh4 is the only legal reply, interposing the queen on the h-file. This defensive move is independently supplied; the source declares mate one step too early.
Rxh4# removes the interposing queen and gives actual mate. Kf7 covers the g-file flight squares and the rook controls the h-file.
branches.classification: selected illustrated source variation with independent forced completion after Rh2+
branches.explanation: Rxh4# removes the interposing queen and gives actual mate. Kf7 covers the g-file flight squares and the rook controls the h-file.

branches.title: Approach the king one tempo too soon
commentary: Compare the source’s premature king approach while the pawns are still on d4 and e3.
Kf7 gives away the forced win. The mating threats arrive before the pawns have advanced to the useful squares.
d3 is the source’s illustrated reply, but it gives White a winning chance again. For example, Rb6 preserves a win in this exact position; the source’s following rook move fails to exploit it.
Ra4 threatens Rh4 mate but gives back that renewed winning chance. The exact position becomes drawn again; a plausible mating threat is not enough.
Kh6 meets the threat and preserves the draw. This source sequence contains two outcome reversals, so it must not be taught as best play by both sides.
branches.explanation: Kh6 meets the threat and preserves the draw. This source sequence contains two outcome reversals, so it must not be taught as best play by both sides.

branches.title: Move the king instead of promoting
commentary: This independently selected representative continuation tests the source’s alternative: Black moves its king rather than promoting.
Kh6 avoids the immediate h-file mate but abandons the e-pawn.
Rxe2 removes Black’s final pawn. White has a checked winning rook-versus-king ending; the lesson stops before assuming a particular mating technique.
branches.classification: independent alternative with representative legal replies
branches.explanation: Rxe2 removes Black’s final pawn. White has a checked winning rook-versus-king ending; the lesson stops before assuming a particular mating technique.

branches.title: Black advances the other pawn to hold the draw
commentary: This independently selected defense compares best resistance after the premature king move.
Kf7 gives away the win, but Black must respond accurately to retain the draw.
e2 is the drawing reply. Black advances the leading pawn before committing d4, denying White the same favorable waiting-move arrangement. The branch ends at this exactly checked draw.
branches.classification: independent alternative with representative legal replies
branches.explanation: After Kf7, ...e2 holds the draw; the source instead shows ...d3, which lets White win again.

exercises.prompt: Why help Black get closer to promotion?
exercises.answer: The extra tempo puts the pawns on d2 and e2. After Rxd2, promoting the e-pawn clears the second rank for Rh2 mate.

exercises.prompt: Why does a new queen fail to help?
exercises.answer: It is not check, and it leaves e2. Rh2+ wins, although the queen can still interpose on h4; Rxh4 then delivers actual mate.

startContext: Begin from the complete five-piece opening board. The source’s waiting move, premature king approach and promotion attack are reconstructed from saved images. The king-retreat completion, drawing defense and forced ...Qh4 Rxh4# finish are explicitly independent.
verification_scope: Saved board images reviewed manually. Every encoded intermediate position and endpoint is checked against the tablebase. Selected instructive variations, not an exhaustive tree of all legal defenses.

sourceCorrections.claim: After Kf7, the illustrated ...d3 and Ra4 demonstrate that White can achieve at best a draw.
sourceCorrections.correction: Kf7 draws, but ...d3 gives White a win again (Rb6 is one winning move). Ra4 then throws that win away and ...Kh6 holds. The independent ...e2 defense demonstrates a draw without those reversals. The general connected-pawn rule is a heuristic; exact king placement and mating threats decide this position.
Rh2+ wins but is not mate: ...Qh4 is the sole legal reply, then Rxh4# is actual mate. The last two plies are an independently supplied forced completion.
